# Adamo Lab — Coding & Data Management Guidelines
> 33 rules adopted by the lab. An agent working in a lab repository should follow every rule below. Rules are identified by ID (S1, V3, ...); cite the ID when you apply or flag one.
Ratified 2026-07-08. Full handbook: guidelines.pdf

## Repository & Project Structure

### S1 — One repo per project, not per person

The work survives the author leaving. Code belongs to the project, not to whoever wrote it. When someone graduates, their scripts stay findable and runnable instead of disappearing onto a personal laptop.

```
adamolab/                  # one GitHub org
├── reaction-time-study/   # one repo per project
├── eye-tracking-2026/
└── saccade-model/
```

### S2 — Standard top-level layout

You find things without asking anyone. Give every repo the same skeleton: README, data/, src/, results/, and an environment lock. Open any project and you know where the code, data pointers, and outputs live.

```
saccade-model/
├── README.md
├── data/            # or a pointer to storage
├── src/
├── results/
└── environment.yml
```

### S3 — No data committed to git

Git chokes on large binaries. Git diffs text well and binaries badly. Commit a few gigabytes and clones crawl, history bloats, and you cannot rewind. Keep data in real storage and version it with a tool built for the job.

```bash
# .gitignore
data/
*.h5

# version data with DVC instead of git
dvc add data/raw.h5
```

### S4 — README answers three questions

New members onboard without you. Cover what the project is, how to set up the environment, and how to run it end to end. A newcomer should reach a first result without messaging you.

```markdown
# Saccade Model
**What:** fits saccade latency from eye-tracking data.
**Setup:** `conda env create -f environment.yml`
**Run:** `make all`
```

## Version Control

### V1 — All project code under git

The throwaway script made a figure. The one-off that produced Figure 3 is the one you need again for the revision. Track everything from the first commit. It costs nothing and saves the panic later.

```bash
git init
git add analysis.py figures.R
git commit -m "Initial analysis pipeline"
```

### V3 — Main branch always runs

A colleague may pull at any moment. Keep main runnable at all times. Do risky work on a branch and merge only once it passes. Whoever pulls next inherits working code, not your half-finished state.

```bash
git switch -c fix-outlier-filter
# ...work, run tests...
git switch main
git merge fix-outlier-filter   # only once green
```

### V4 — Shared remote org, not personal accounts

Access outlives any one person. Host repos under a lab organization instead of a personal account. Permissions and continuity then survive graduations, and nobody chases a former student for admin rights.

```bash
# lab org remote, not a personal account
git remote add origin \
  git@github.com:adamolab/saccade-model.git
```

## Environments & Reproducibility

### E1 — Every project pins its environment

'Works on my machine' is not a result. Record exact package versions so the analysis runs the same next year and on a colleague's laptop. Leave the environment unpinned and it drifts until the numbers stop matching.

```yaml
# environment.yml
name: saccade
dependencies:
  - python=3.11
  - numpy=1.26.4
  - pandas=2.2.1
```

### E2 — One command reproduces the main result

Untested reproducibility is a guess. Wire the pipeline behind a single entry point: a Makefile, a script, or a workflow. If rerunning the analysis needs tribal knowledge, it does not reproduce.

```makefile
all: results/fig1.pdf

results/fig1.pdf: src/plot.py data/clean.csv
	python src/plot.py
```

### E3 — Set and record a random seed

Same input should give the same figure. Fix and log the seed wherever randomness touches results: splits, initialization, sampling. Skip it and two identical runs disagree, and you cannot tell signal from noise.

```python
import numpy as np, torch
SEED = 42
np.random.seed(SEED)
torch.manual_seed(SEED)
```

### E4 — Scripts or clean notebooks for published results

Out-of-order cells lie. Explore in notebooks, but generate any published number from a script or a notebook that runs top to bottom without error. Hidden execution order is where mistakes hide.

```bash
# run a notebook top-to-bottom, no manual state
jupyter nbconvert --to notebook --execute \
  --output out.ipynb analysis.ipynb
```

## Coding Conventions

### C1 — Auto-formatter per language

No human should format code. Hand formatting to a tool so nobody burns a review comment on whitespace. Consistent style also keeps diffs focused on real changes instead of reflows.

```bash
black src/                          # Python
Rscript -e 'styler::style_dir("R")'  # R
shfmt -w scripts/                   # Shell
```

### C2 — Descriptive names beat comments that explain bad names

A good name never goes stale. subject_reaction_times explains itself. srt needs a comment, and that comment drifts from the code the moment someone edits nearby.

```python
# bad
srt = df[df.srt > 0.1]
# good
valid = trials[trials.reaction_time > 0.1]
```

### C3 — No hard-coded absolute paths

/Users/alice/ breaks for everyone else. Absolute paths fail the instant a second person runs the code. Use relative paths or one path variable at the top so the project moves between machines.

```python
# bad
df = pd.read_csv("/Users/alice/data/rt.csv")
# good
from pathlib import Path
DATA = Path(__file__).parent / "data"
df = pd.read_csv(DATA / "rt.csv")
```

### C4 — Functions for anything used more than twice

Fix it once, not in five places. Copy, paste, tweak, and now four near-copies drift apart. Pull anything you write a third time into one function so a fix lands everywhere at once.

```python
def zscore(x):
    return (x - x.mean()) / x.std()

rt_z  = zscore(df.rt)
amp_z = zscore(df.amp)
```

### C5 — Config at the top, not scattered

Changing a run should take one edit. Keep parameters, paths, and thresholds in one block or file instead of sprinkled through the code. Tuning an experiment then means editing one spot.

```python
# config.py
RAW    = "data/raw.csv"
RT_MIN = 0.1
N_BOOT = 10_000
```

## Naming Conventions

### N1 — Python identifiers follow PEP 8

The linter and every reader expect it. snake_case for variables, functions, and modules. PascalCase for classes. UPPER_SNAKE_CASE for constants.

```python
rt_min = 0.1                 # variable: snake_case
RT_MAX = 2.0                 # constant: UPPER_SNAKE
def clean_trials(raw): ...   # function: snake_case
class SaccadeModel: ...      # class: PascalCase
```

### N2 — R identifiers follow the tidyverse style

A dot means an S3 method, so avoid dots. snake_case for variables and functions. Skip dots in new names. PascalCase for R6 and S4 classes.

```r
rt_min <- 0.1                       # snake_case
clean_trials <- function(raw) { }   # snake_case
# avoid: clean.trials  (dot = S3 method)
```

### N4 — Shell: snake_case locals, UPPER_SNAKE exported

Hyphens are illegal in shell variable names. Local variables and functions use snake_case. Environment and exported variables use UPPER_SNAKE_CASE.

```bash
DATA_ROOT=/mnt/labshare      # exported: UPPER_SNAKE
clean_trials() {             # function: snake_case
  local raw_file="$1"        # local: snake_case
}
```

### N5 — Constants and classes are cross-language

Keep the shouted categories recognizable. Constants and environment variables are UPPER_SNAKE_CASE in every language. Classes and types are PascalCase in every language.

```
UPPER_SNAKE_CASE   constants, env vars   (all languages)
PascalCase         classes, types        (all languages)
```

### N6 — Filesystem names are lowercase

Data/ and data/ collide across machines. Lowercase every file and directory name. Linux sees two folders where macOS sees one, and that gap corrupts a shared repo.

```bash
mkdir raw-data        # good
mkdir Raw_Data        # collides on case-insensitive macOS
```

### N7 — No spaces in names

Spaces force quoting and break scripts. Use a hyphen or underscore instead of a space in any file or directory name.

```
eye-tracking-data.csv     # good
eye tracking data.csv     # needs quoting everywhere
```

### N8 — Restrict names to a-z 0-9 - _ .

Other characters are illegal or shell-special. Colons and backslashes are illegal on Windows. The characters & * ? ! carry shell meaning. A leading hyphen looks like a command flag.

```
s01_congruent_v02.csv     # good
s01:congruent (2)!.csv    # illegal on Windows, shell-hostile
```

### N9 — Avoid reserved names, keep paths short

Windows chokes on con, nul, and long paths. Never name a file con, prn, aux, nul, com1, or lpt1. Keep total path length well under 260 characters.

```
reserved on Windows: con prn aux nul com1..com9 lpt1..lpt9
keep the full path under 260 characters
```

### N10 — Repositories and branches use kebab-case

Matches GitHub, URLs, and the ecosystem. Name repositories and git branches in lowercase kebab-case.

```bash
adamolab/eye-tracking-2026         # repo
git switch -c fix-outlier-filter   # branch
```

### N11 — Directories use kebab-case

Readable in a URL and a terminal. Name directories in lowercase kebab-case.

```
saccade-model/
├── raw-data/
├── figure-scripts/
└── clean-output/
```

### N12 — Script files follow language import rules

Python cannot import a hyphenated module. Python and R modules use snake_case so they stay importable. Standalone shell tools use kebab-case, matching how you type the command.

```
data_cleaning.py     # Python module, importable
clean_data.R         # R script
run-analysis.sh      # shell tool, a CLI command
```

### N14 — Config keys use snake_case

They map straight onto code variables. Keys in YAML, TOML, or JSON use snake_case so they line up with the Python and R variables that read them.

```yaml
# config.yml
rt_min: 0.1
n_boot: 10000
data_root: /mnt/labshare
```

## Data Management

### D2 — Consistent, sortable file naming

final_final2 is where projects die. Name files so machines can read them: ISO dates, no spaces, zero-padded versions. They then sort correctly and a script can glob them.

```
2026-07-08_s01_congruent_v02.csv
2026-07-08_s02_incongruent_v02.csv
# not:  final data (2)!!.csv
```

### D3 — Every dataset has a data dictionary

Data without metadata turns to noise. Ship a description of each field with the data: meaning, units, collection date, and who collected it. Skip it and your own spreadsheet baffles you within a year.

```
# data_dictionary.md
rt        Reaction time, seconds
accuracy  1 = correct, 0 = error
subject   Anonymized ID (s01..s40)
```

### D5 — 3-2-1 backup for irreplaceable raw data

Irreplaceable means irreplaceable. Keep three copies, on two kinds of media, with one off-site. Data you cannot recollect earns at least a primary plus one automated backup.

```
copy 1  /mnt/labshare/saccade     primary
copy 2  external HDD              weekly rsync
copy 3  institutional cloud      offsite
```

### D7 — Sensitive data documented and access-controlled

Law and ethics require it. De-identify personal data where you can, lock down access where you cannot, and write down how you handle it.

```bash
python deidentify.py raw/ -o safe/
chmod 700 safe/            # owner-only access
```

## Collaboration & Handover

### H1 — Leaving-the-lab checklist

Most lost work traces to a departure. Before anyone leaves: push the code, pin the environment, document where the data lives, and update the README. The alternative is a low bus factor and a scramble after they are gone.

```
[ ] code pushed to origin
[ ] environment.yml committed
[ ] data location in README
[ ] README run steps current
```

## Not adopted

These were proposed and vetoed. Do not enforce them, and do not present them as lab policy.

- **V2 — Commit messages say why, not just what** (vetoed): git log is your real lab notebook.
- **N3 — MATLAB identifiers follow MathWorks style** (vetoed): The file name must match the function.
- **N13 — Data files use the fielded convention** (vetoed): Sort by date, glob by field.
- **D1 — Raw data is read-only, never edited in place** (vetoed): You cannot un-overwrite raw data.
- **D4 — Single source of truth for storage** (vetoed): No more 'which copy is current?'
- **D6 — Provenance link from result to data and code** (vetoed): A reviewer will ask two years later.
- **H2 — Code review for shared or published pipelines** (vetoed): Cheap insurance where it counts.

## How to use this file

You are expected to audit, not to edit. For each rule ID report PASS, FAIL, or
N/A, and name the file or command that proves it. Do not invent rules, do not
report anything from the "Not adopted" list as a failure, and say "cannot verify"
for anything that depends on facts outside the repository (D5 backups, D7 access
control, whether a documented storage path is still live).
